301.event_title: Grant offers generous terms to Lee's army at Appomattox
301.place: McLean House, Appomattox Court House, Virginia, United States
301.event: With the Confederate Army of Northern Virginia surrounded, General Robert E. Lee met General Ulysses S. Grant in Wilmer McLean's parlour to surrender. Grant's terms paroled the Confederate soldiers and sent them home rather than to prison camps, allowed officers to keep their side arms, horses and baggage, and permitted men who owned horses or mules to take them home. Grant also offered 25,000 rations for Lee's hungry troops, and at the end of the meeting he and his staff raised their hats to Lee as he rode away.
301.explanation: At the moment when Grant held complete power over a defeated enemy that had cost his side dearly, he chose restraint and generosity instead of punishment.
301.tie_back: The kural says the true test of restraining anger comes where one has the power to make it effective, and Grant, with Lee's army at his mercy, showed exactly that restraint.
301._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of restraint exercised from a position of overwhelming power, though the sources describe Grant's generosity rather than any anger he had to suppress.

302.event_title: John McEnroe is defaulted from the Australian Open
302.event: Playing Mikael Pernfors in the fourth round of the 1990 Australian Open, John McEnroe received a warning for glaring at a lineswoman and then a point penalty for cracking his racket. When he protested and swore at the Grand Slam chief of supervisors, the umpire defaulted him from the match. He became the first player since 1963 to be disqualified from a Grand Slam tournament for misconduct, and afterwards accepted that he had himself to blame.
302.explanation: McEnroe's anger was aimed at officials he had no power to overrule, so it could change nothing except the outcome for himself.
302.tie_back: The kural says anger directed where it cannot prevail only harms oneself, and McEnroe's outburst against the officials cost him the match he had been leading.
302._accuracy_note: Illustrates the kural's first line well, but not its second line about anger against the weak being the worst evil.

303.event_title: The Peace of Westphalia declares perpetual oblivion and amnesty
303.place: Munster and Osnabruck, Westphalia, Germany (Holy Roman Empire)
303.event: The treaties of Munster and Osnabruck, together known as the Peace of Westphalia, ended the Thirty Years' War. Their second articles declared that there should be on both sides a perpetual oblivion and amnesty for all hostile acts committed since the beginning of the troubles. Grievances and claims arising from the war were to be buried in perpetual oblivion so that they could not be used against the other side.
303.explanation: After decades of devastating war, the peacemakers wrote into law that past injuries must be forgotten, recognising that remembered grievances would only breed new conflict.
303.tie_back: The kural asks us to let go of anger toward anyone and forget it, because every evil is born from anger, and the Westphalian treaties made such forgetting a binding legal duty.
303._accuracy_note: A strong match for the kural's call to forget grievances, though the treaty speaks of hostile acts rather than of the emotion of anger itself.

304.event_title: Seneca writes On Anger for his brother Novatus
304.event: The Stoic philosopher Lucius Annaeus Seneca wrote the treatise De Ira (On Anger), addressed to his elder brother Novatus, who had asked how anger might be soothed. In it Seneca described anger as a kind of brief madness, more conspicuous than other passions because it shows in the face and boils forth the more plainly the greater it is. He argued that anger cannot be moderated and must be eliminated rather than managed.
304.explanation: Seneca's treatise is one of the earliest sustained arguments that anger disfigures the person who feels it and is an enemy to be removed entirely.
304.tie_back: The kural says anger kills both the smile on the face and the joy in the heart and asks whether there is any greater enemy, and Seneca likewise portrayed anger as visibly ruining the face and overthrowing the mind.
304._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the treatise is a documented event that argues the kural's point, rather than an episode showing anger destroying someone's happiness.

305.event_title: Surgeon John Hunter collapses during a heated hospital board meeting
305.event: John Hunter, the leading surgeon and anatomist of his day, had long suffered from angina pectoris. On 16 October 1793, during a meeting of the board of governors of St George's Hospital, he was engaged in a heated discussion over the admission of students when he collapsed and died. His collections later passed to the Royal College of Surgeons, and he was reburied in Westminster Abbey in 1859.
305.explanation: Hunter's death in the middle of a heated quarrel has long been cited as an example of how anger can endanger the person who gives way to it.
305.tie_back: The kural says that if you do not guard yourself against anger it will destroy you yourself, and Hunter's life ended in the very moment of a bitter dispute.
305._accuracy_note: A strong illustration, though the sources describe the cause of death differently and do not prove that anger alone caused it.

306.event_title: William Bligh is cast adrift after the mutiny on the Bounty
306.event: Lieutenant William Bligh, commander of HMS Bounty, had become enraged at his crew's seamanship and had fallen out with his first mate and longtime friend Fletcher Christian. On 28 April 1789 Christian and his supporters seized the ship and set Bligh and 18 loyal men adrift in a small open launch. Bligh navigated about 3,600 miles to Timor, but historians note that while he used physical punishment less than other captains, he was verbally and personally abusive, and later he faced a court-martial (and acquittal) for abusive language.
306.explanation: Bligh's skill and courage were never in doubt, but his abusive temper turned his own officers and crew, the people who should have carried him safely home, against him.
306.tie_back: The kural says anger is a fire that burns even the raft of kinsmen and friends that would carry a person through life, and Bligh's anger literally cost him his ship and left him adrift in an open boat.
306._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of anger destroying the very companions who sustain a person, though historians also cite other causes of the mutiny, such as the attractions of life on Tahiti.

307.event_title: General Patton's slapping incidents in Sicily
307.event: During the Sicily campaign, Lieutenant General George S. Patton visited army hospitals and struck two soldiers suffering from what would today be diagnosed as combat stress, accusing them of cowardice. When the incidents became known, General Eisenhower reprimanded him and he was ordered to apologise personally to the two soldiers and to his entire Seventh Army. He lost his Mediterranean command and was passed over for command of American ground forces in the Normandy invasion, which went instead to Omar Bradley.
307.explanation: Patton treated harsh anger as a tool of leadership, and the episode badly damaged the career of one of the most gifted commanders of the war.
307.tie_back: The kural says ruin surely comes to one who treats anger as something valuable, just as the hand that strikes the ground cannot escape injury, and Patton's blows rebounded on his own career.
307._accuracy_note: A strong fit: the angry blows harmed the striker's own standing, though Patton's later wartime successes show the ruin was not total.

308.event_title: Eva Mozes Kor forgives her Nazi persecutors at Auschwitz
308.event: As a ten-year-old twin, Eva Mozes Kor had been subjected to Josef Mengele's experiments at Auschwitz, where her parents and two older sisters were killed. On the 50th anniversary of the camp's liberation, she returned to Auschwitz with Dr. Hans Munch, a former camp doctor who signed a document attesting to the operation of the gas chambers, and she read and signed her own declaration forgiving the Nazis. Her decision drew criticism from some fellow survivors, but she said it freed her from the pain she had carried for fifty years.
308.explanation: Kor chose to give up resentment toward those who had inflicted the worst imaginable suffering on her family, and she described the act as her own liberation.
308.tie_back: The kural says that even when someone does you harm as painful as being plunged into a blazing fire, it is good, if you can, to refrain from anger toward them, and Kor did so after enduring one of history's greatest injuries.
308._accuracy_note: Very close to the kural, which concedes that such restraint may exceed ordinary capacity; her forgiveness remains controversial among survivors.

309.event_title: Bjorn Borg, the Ice Man of tennis, wins five straight Wimbledon titles
309.event: Swedish player Bjorn Borg won the Wimbledon singles championship five years in a row from 1976 to 1980 and six French Open titles, and was known as the Ice Man for never letting opponents see what he was feeling on court. Borg later recalled that he had been suspended as a 13-year-old for bad behaviour and afterwards kept his emotions inside, receiving penalty points only once in his professional career. He retired at 26 with 11 major singles titles.
309.explanation: Borg's refusal to let anger take hold during matches was regarded by himself and others as a central strength of his game.
309.tie_back: The kural promises that one who never lets anger enter the mind will attain what he sets his heart on, and Borg's famous composure accompanied one of the most successful careers in tennis.
309._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: Borg said he still felt anger inside and controlled its expression, whereas the kural asks that anger not arise even in thought; his teenage suspension is documented in his own recollection.

310.event_title: Tolstoy makes Do not be angry the first commandment of his faith
310.event: In What I Believe, written in 1884, Leo Tolstoy set out the teaching he drew from the Sermon on the Mount, naming as Jesus' first commandment that one must live in peace with all and never regard anger as justified. His later Christianity stressed five tenets, beginning with be not angry and including do not resist evil and love your enemies, and his doctrine of nonviolent nonresistance went on to inspire Gandhi. Tolstoy renounced the church's rituals and was excommunicated by the Russian Orthodox Church in 1901.
310.explanation: One of the world's great novelists placed the complete renunciation of anger at the head of a moral teaching that he presented as a renunciant's way of life.
310.tie_back: The kural says those who have wholly renounced anger are equal to those who have renounced the world, and Tolstoy built a renouncer's creed whose very first rule was to give up anger.
310._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Tolstoy taught the renunciation of anger, but Britannica notes he did not succeed in living fully by his own teachings, and the kural's first line about the excessively angry being like the dead is not shown.
